question:
Which of the below has not undergone trisyllabic laxing during its sound development: 

southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is "shadow". It derives from Old English sceadu (with a short vowel already in the disyllabic form), and unlike cases such as divine/divinity or serene/serenity, there is no evidence of a prior long vowel that would have been subject to trisyllabic laxing when an extra syllable was added. The other words all show clear laxing alternations traceable to that historical process.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: After thinking through the examples, I believe "shadow" is the one that hasn't undergone trisyllabic laxing. It derives directly from Old English sceadu (a disyllabic form) without a clear trisyllabic intermediate stage that would trigger the shortening process, whereas the others all involve derivatives or inflections creating three or more syllables (e.g., south + ern yielding southern with lax /ʌ/, or serene to serenity with the shift to /ɛ/). This seems consistent with how the rule applies mainly in morphological derivations rather than inherited short forms like shadow.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer here is shadow. Trisyllabic laxing applies to cases where a tense vowel shortens before two following syllables in derived forms, as seen in southern (from south + -ern, with the vowel laxing to /ʌ/), derivative (from derive, /aɪ/ to /ɪ/), serenity (from serene, /iː/ to /ɛ/), gratitude (from grateful/grate, with the relevant vowel adjustment), and pleasant (from please, /iː/ to /ɛ/). Shadow, however, derives from Old English sceadu with an already short /a/ that shows no evidence of a prior tense vowel undergoing this specific change in its development, making it the outlier.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is shadow. Most of the others show clear shortening of a historically long vowel in a trisyllabic context (southern from sūþerne with ū > ʌ, derivative from dērīvāre with ī > ɪ, serenity from sērenitās with ē > ɛ, gratitude from grātitūdō with ā > æ). Pleasant is a bit tricky because of its French source, but the vowel alternation still fits the pattern. Shadow, by contrast, descends from OE sceadu (already short æ/a), and its modern form never had a long vowel that would have been eligible for trisyllabic laxing in the first place, so it simply stayed as it was.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is shadow. Looking at the etymologies, southern shows the expected laxing of /uː/ to /ʌ/ in the trisyllabic form, derivative has the /aɪ/ to /ɪ/ shift, serenity the /iː/ to /ɛ/, pleasant the /eː/ to /ɛ/, and gratitude the /eɪ/ to /æ/. Shadow, by contrast, descends from OE sceadu with an already short /a/ that never participated in the later Middle English laxing rule triggered by following syllables, so it stands apart from the others.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: After thinking through the historical vowel changes, I lean toward "gratitude" as the one that hasn't undergone trisyllabic laxing. The others all show the classic pattern of a tense vowel in a base form becoming lax when suffixes create a trisyllabic (or effectively trisyllabic) environment, like serene/serenity or derive/derivative. Southern alternates with south in a way that fits the laxing environment historically, pleasant reflects the lax /ɛ/ from please, and shadow has a related form that suggests the same shortening. Gratitude, by contrast, seems to have kept its vowel quality stable from the Latin source without that specific shift applying in its English development.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow

Trisyllabic laxing is the English phonological/historical shortening/laxing of a stressed long vowel when the word is made polysyllabic by suffixation, e.g. /iː/ > /ɪ/ ~ /ɛ/, /aɪ/ > /ɪ/, /eɪ/ > /ɛ/ ~ /æ/ in a stressed syllable that is followed by two or more unstressed syllables.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛn.ə.ti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /ɡreɪt/  ~ grateful /ˈɡreɪt.fəl/ > gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/ in the three-syllable form
* south /saʊθ/ > southern /ˈsʌð.ən/ ~ /ˈsaʊ.ðərn/ shows the same reduction of the stem vowel in the suffixed compound.

The vowel in shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ is not a case of a stem vowel being laxed by suffixation. Shadow < OE sceadu, sceadwe, is historically distinct from the /eɪ/ stem shade < OE sceard. The /æ/ of shadow is inherited from the Old English stem and is not the product of a trisyllabic laxing of a long /eɪ/ /aɪ/ /iː/ etc. in a derived polysyllabic form. It is the only item in the set whose present vowel quality is not explicable as the outcome of trisyllabic laxing of a shorter base.

The disyllabic items southern and pleasant also show vowel reduction, but the classic textbook trisyllabic laxing cases in the list are derivative, serenity and gratitude.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Southern is the clear textbook non-case.

The classic trisyllabic laxing change is tense → lax of the stressed vowel when the stem is lengthened to a stress – penultimate + post-tonic syllable environment, e.g.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛn.ɪ.ti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

All three are genuinely trisyllabic / polysyllabic derivatives with the regular tense→lax shift in the stressed syllable.

Southern /ˈsaʊ.ðən/ is a disyllabic south + -ern formation and the stressed vowel is phonologically identical to its monosyllabic base south /saʊθ/ : /aʊ/ > /aʊ/. No tense→lax development of the type that is described as trisyllabic laxing has taken place in the word. 

Pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/ and shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ are also disyllabic, so by definition they cannot be instances of trisyllabic laxing, and the /iː/ > /ɛ/ and /eɪ/ > /æ/ changes they show are the ordinary OE/ME shortening that accompanies -ant / -ow, not the trisyllabic environment-driven laxing seen in derivative, serenity and gratitude. Southern is the only item in the set which retains an unchanged, non-laxed stressed vowel from its base.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow

shortening that appears when a base with a long/stressed vowel is
extended by a  -ic/-ity/-ive/-ant/-tude  etc. suffix so that the
stressed vowel comes to be followed by at least one unstressed
syllable in a word of three or more syllables, typically penultimate
stress.

* derive /dɪˈvaɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛn.ə.ti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /greɪt/ > gratitude /ˈgræt.ɪ.tuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/

In each case the vowel that is long in the disyllabic base is
shortened / laxed in the longer derived form.

shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ is a disyllabic root.  The modern /æ/ goes back to OE
sceadu /skæːdu/ and the OE > ME change /eɪ/ shade > /æ/ shadow is the
regular monophthongisation / shortening of the disyllabic noun/verb

10.text:
The classic three-syllable condition is a shortening / laxing of a long
stressed vowel when it is followed by two or more unstressed syllables,
normally with the stress antepenultimate, e.g.

* grate /greɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtud/
* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/

and so on.  In the set

* southern /ˈsʌð.ən/
* pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/
* shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/

are disyllabic.  They show the regular shortening/lowering that goes
with the -ern/-ant/-ow suffixes but they are not three-syllable
words and hence they are not instances of the antepenultimate
trisyllabic laxing rule proper.  Of the disyllabic Germanic items the
clearest non-example is shadow.  Etymologically *shadow* < OE sceadu
is the base of shade and the /æ/ is the historic short vowel of the
word; it is not a laxed reflex of a long /eɪ/ under the three-syllable
condition.  The same is true of southern and pleasant.  The only
genuine three-syllable, initial-stress laxing in the list is gratitude
– c.f. grate /ɡreɪt/ > /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/ – derivative and serenity showing

shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is a two-syllable formation from OE sceadu.  The monophthong

long /aː/ ~ /ɑː/ of the Latin base, the regular trisyllabic outcome.
* southern < south /saʊθ/ > southern /ˈsʌðən/. The stem is lengthened by
-ern and the vowel is reduced/laxed in the polysyllabic form.

Shadow is an inherited West Germanic word OE sceadu / skædu /. It is
disyllabic /ˈʃædoʊ/ today and it is disyllabic in its history, with an
originally short stressed vowel *a* > /æ/. There is no Romance long vowel
that is shortened by the addition of a third syllable, and no trisyllabic
laxing environment is ever met in its development. The same formal
observation holds for the other disyllabic items southern and pleasant,
shadow being the prototypical native Germanic non-la xed example of the set.
public_text.6:
The classic environment for the English trisyllabic – or
pre-tonic – shortening is a long stressed vowel which is followed in the
same phonological word by two or more unstressed syllables.  The
phonetic effect is the familiar /iː eː eɪ oʊ aɪ/ → /ɪ ɛ æ ɔ a/ type
shortening which is seen in the Romance loans

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛ.nə.ti/
* grate /ɡreɪt/  > gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/

and, in the same phonetic guise, in the disyllabic loans pleasant
/ˈpliːz/ > /ˈplɛz.ənt/ and shadow /ʃeɪd/ > /ˈʃæ.doʊ/.

southern /ˈsʌ.ðən/ is the odd case.  It is a disyllabic Germanic
formation south + -ern and the stressed vowel is not a long
monophthong which has been laxed in a trisyllabic environment at all.
OE sūþ /suːθ/ > ME south /sauθ/ > ModE /saʊθ/ gives in the derivative
southern a diphthongal reduction /aʊ/ > /ʌ/ with loss of the second
element of the diphthong, i.e. a normal unstressed-syllable reduction
/ south-ern /, not the regular /iː eː eɪ oʊ aɪ/ → lax shortening that
is the textbook trisyllabic laxing.  In strict syllable-count terms
pleasant /ˈplɛ.zənt/ and shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ are likewise disyllabic and
therefore do not meet the “stressed vowel followed by two unstressed
syllables” environment of the historical rule, the first being the
commonly quoted Romance disyllabic shortening parallel to the
trisyllabic cases.
public_text.10:
The classic three-syllable condition is a shortening / laxing of a long
stressed vowel when it is followed by two or more unstressed syllables,
normally with the stress antepenultimate, e.g.

* grate /greɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtud/
* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/

and so on.  In the set

* southern /ˈsʌð.ən/
* pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/
* shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/

are disyllabic.  They show the regular shortening/lowering that goes
with the -ern/-ant/-ow suffixes but they are not three-syllable
words and hence they are not instances of the antepenultimate
trisyllabic laxing rule proper.  Of the disyllabic Germanic items the
clearest non-example is shadow.  Etymologically *shadow* < OE sceadu
is the base of shade and the /æ/ is the historic short vowel of the
word; it is not a laxed reflex of a long /eɪ/ under the three-syllable
condition.  The same is true of southern and pleasant.  The only
genuine three-syllable, initial-stress laxing in the list is gratitude
– c.f. grate /ɡreɪt/ > /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/ – derivative and serenity showing
the same vowel-shortening process on the stressed penultimate.
public_text.12:
Trisyllabic laxing is the historic shortening/laxing of a tense/stressed vowel
when the stressed syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables,
e.g.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ ~ grateful /ˈɡreɪtfəl/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/

and the same type of development that is usually illustrated with
please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/.

All of these are genuine polysyllabic derivatives in which a historically
tense stressed vowel is laxed/shortened in the extended form.

shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is a two-syllable formation from OE sceadu.  The monophthong
/æ/ in the modern form is not the product of a vowel that was laxed under a
tri-syllabic environment, it is the regular reflex of the OE vowel and the
/eɪ/ ~ /æ/ alternation with shade /ʃeɪd/ is the normal pre-consonantal
lowering/assimilation of the word family.  The word never has a
stressed-vowel-plus-two-unstressed-syllables environment in which the
classic trisyllabic laxing could apply.

Southern /ˈsʌðən/ and pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ are in the same disyllabic
class; shadow is the clearest disyllabic, non-trisyllabic example in the
set.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which item has not undergone the historical tense → lax shortening that is described as trisyllabic laxing. The discussion is split on how strictly to apply the three-syllable environment.

Core claim that is repeated by most colleagues:
* derivative /dɪˈraɪv/ > /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serenity /səˈriːn/ > /səˈrɛn.ə.ti/  /iː/ > /ɛ/
* gratitude /ɡreɪt/ ~ grateful > /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/
are canonical three-syllable, antepenultimate-stress laxings. Those three are consistently treated as genuine cases.

The remaining three are disyllabic in Modern English:
southern /ˈsʌð.ən/, pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/, shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/. 
Colleague 10, 11, 12, 3, 6, 8 note that by strict syllable count they cannot be instances of the classic stressed-vowel-plus-two-unstressed-syllables rule. Many still call pleasant /pliːz/ > /ˈplɛzənt/ and southern /saʊθ/ > /ˈsʌðən/ regular polysyllabic shortening/lowering that is often lumped with trisyllabic laxing in textbooks, while shadow is Germanic.

The key distinguishing evidence for shadow:
* shadow < OE sceadu /skæːdu/, cognate with sceadwe, historically a short /a/ stem. No prior long /eɪ/ or /aɪ/ stem that could be laxed.
* The /æ/ of shadow is not a laxed reflex of the /eɪ/ of shade < OE sceard; the two are separate historical roots. No suffix-driven environment ever created a stressed vowel + two unstressed syllables for the word.
Hence shadow is the only item whose present vowel quality is inherited short and not explicable as the outcome of laxing a historically tense vowel under suffixation.

Competing minority views noted:
* Colleague 1 argues gratitude has kept its vowel stable from Latin and is the non-case, and treats southern, pleasant and shadow as showing laxing.
* Colleague 11 and Colleague 6 argue southern /saʊθ/ > /ˈsʌð.ən/ retains /aʊ/ essentially unchanged and is the textbook non-case; they treat pleasant and shadow as also disyllabic non-instances.
* Colleague 10 and 12 treat southern and pleasant as disyllabic shortening parallels but still pick shadow as the clearest Germanic non-example.

Unresolved nuance: whether “trisyllabic laxing” is being used strictly as three-syllable shortening, in which southern, pleasant and shadow would all be non-qualifying, or in the looser textbook sense where disyllabic suffixal shortening is included. Under the looser sense, shadow remains the outlier because southern and pleasant do show vowel reduction from a long base while shadow does not.

Current working leaning: shadow is the intended odd one out – no historical long stressed vowel to lax, disyllabic inherited West Germanic with an originally short vowel, versus the genuine trisyllabic cases derivative, serenity, gratitude and the commonly cited disyllabic shortening parallels southern and pleasant.

The process being tested is the historical tense → lax shortening of a stressed vowel that is put in an antepenultimate position by suffixation, canonically /aɪ/ > /ɪ/, /iː/ > /ɛ/, /eɪ/ > /æ/.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnəti/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/

are the textbook three-syllable Romance/Latinate cases with a recoverable long/tense base vowel that is laxed in the extended form.

southern /ˈsʌðən/ < south /saʊθ/ + -ern  /aʊ/ > /ʌ/ and pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ < please /pliːz/ + -ant  /iː/ > /ɛ/ are the standard disyllabic parallels to the same suffix-driven tense-base reduction. They are now disyllabic so they do not meet the strict stressed-vowel-plus-two-unstressed-syllables count, but they do involve laxing of a formerly tense base vowel.

shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ < OE sceadu, sceadwe is different. The modern /æ/ is the regular West Germanic reflex of an inherited historically short stressed *a in a native disyllabic root. There is no recoverable long/tense stressed vowel in the stem of shadow that could be laxed by suffixation, and the word never enters a stressed-vowel-followed-by-two-unstressed-syllables environment. The /eɪ/ ~ /æ/ alternation with shade /ʃeɪd/ is a lexical/historical Germanic length contrast preserved from Old English, not suffix-driven antepenultimate laxing.

Hence shadow is the only item in the set whose present vowel quality is not explicable as the outcome of laxing a historically tense/long stressed vowel at all, the clearest non-instance of trisyllabic laxing.
